assetConcepts.heading: Choose an asset by its job in the game.
assetConcepts.intro: An Asset is an independently created, edited, related, and deliverable unit in a project. Choose the type that matches how the result will be used.
assetConcepts.characterBody: Use Character for a player, enemy, NPC, or animal that needs states, directions, or actions. Describe its identity, body, equipment, animation, canvas, and project perspective.
assetConcepts.objectBody: Use Object for a chest, alchemy table, tree, lamp, furniture, or decoration that is placed, collided with, interacted with, or replaced as one unit. Describe its purpose, size, footprint, view, and visual states.
assetConcepts.tilesetBody: Use Tileset for grid-organized pieces that build floors, walls, platforms, borders, and transitions. Describe materials, grid occupancy, variants, connections, and seamless placement. A complete forest background is Scenery; grass edges and corners for a map are Tileset.
assetConcepts.sceneryTitle: Scenery: a composed scene and its layers
assetConcepts.sceneryBody: Use Scenery for a complete environment image or layered background. Describe place, time, weather, style, layer order, aspect ratio, and parallax behavior. The home page combines sky, wind, and nearby trees to show this layered responsibility.
assetConcepts.sceneryAlt: Animated pixel-art scene showing sky wind and nearby trees layering into a complete background
assetConcepts.uiSetBody: Use UI Set for HUD, menus, panels, buttons, labels, progress bars, badges, and icons. Describe the component list, states, shared visual language, interaction variants, and target resolution. A wooden panel for an inventory is UI Set; a wooden door in the world is Object or Tileset.
assetConcepts.uiSetAlt: Pixel-art UI Set with panels buttons progress bars and icons
assetConcepts.confusingBody: Object is one complete item; Tileset is a repeatable grid unit. Object is one interactive or replaceable world item; Scenery is a composed image and atmosphere. Fixed composition and parallax point to Scenery; endless grid construction points to Tileset. Screen-fixed elements are UI Set, while world-space items are Object. Actions and direction point to Character; decoration points to Object.
assetConcepts.checklistBody: Confirm the delivery unit, whether it belongs to the game world, map grid, or screen, and the context the type requires: perspective and canvas for visual assets, grid rules for Tileset, layers and aspect ratio for Scenery, or components and states for UI Set. The right type describes what the asset does, not only what the image looks like.

directions.heading: Direction count defines how freely a character can move.
directions.intro: A direction is one view of the same character. More directions make movement more natural, but each added view must preserve pose, equipment, and lighting.
directions.match: Match direction count to real movement
directions.twoBody: Use left and right views for side-on characters that move horizontally, such as platformer and side-scrolling action characters.
directions.fourBody: Use front, back, left, and right as the practical starting point for top-down movement.
directions.fourNote: Each view should retain the same silhouette, weapon position, and lighting direction. This swordsman set shows the four cardinal views needed for a top-down character.
directions.eightBody: Add the four diagonals when the game includes diagonal movement, aiming, or smoother turning. Do not select eight directions by default; they need more consistency work.
directions.eightNote: The basketball player set adds north-west, north-east, south-west, and south-east views. Compare each diagonal with its neighboring cardinal directions before using it in animation.

perspective.heading: Choose the camera for your world before generating its assets.
perspective.intro: Perspective controls how players read space. Decide it before creating characters, props, and scenery so every asset can share the same visual rules.
perspective.topDownBody: Use top-down when players need to see terrain, nearby opponents, and movement around a character. It is a practical fit for action RPGs and tactical maps.
perspective.sideOnBody: Use Side-On when jumping height, horizontal rhythm, and silhouette readability drive the experience. It suits platformers and side-scrolling action games.
perspective.isometricBody: Use isometric when the scene needs both building volume and a readable map layout. It suits simulation and strategy scenes.
perspective.keepBody: Once you choose a perspective, include it in every character, prop, and environment request. Mixing Top-Down characters with Side-On props makes the asset set difficult to combine, even when colour and style match.
perspective.topDownAlt: Top-Down game scene showing terrain, props, and characters from above
perspective.sideOnAlt: Side-On game scene showing a character and platform environment
perspective.isometricAlt: Isometric game scene showing buildings and terrain at an angled view

reference.heading: A reference is a visual constraint, not just inspiration.
reference.introBody: A clear reference tells the generator which proportions, colour treatment, silhouette, and equipment must remain consistent. Start with one primary image that establishes the result you want.
reference.imageAlt: Pixel-art farm scene reference showing paths, buildings, crops, trees, and water
reference.chooseTitle: Choose references that answer a specific question
reference.choose1: Keep the character's proportions, clothing silhouette, and key equipment.
reference.choose2: Match lighting direction and colour treatment to the target asset.
reference.choose3: Use a clean image with an unobstructed, generously framed subject.
reference.choose4: Add supporting references only for local material or equipment detail.
reference.choose5: When images disagree, state which one defines the final result.
reference.promptBody: Use the reference to establish the visual language, then name the details that cannot change. If a weapon, hairstyle, or colour matters, include it in the prompt. This keeps a supporting image from accidentally changing the primary reference's perspective or style.
reference.differenceBody: This reference defines the target character's identity and visual style. The two results below target the same role.
reference.resultImageAlt: Pixel-art farming game reference for a character generation example
reference.resultNote: Both results use the same prompt. The first uses the prompt alone; the second adds this image as a reference, producing stronger visual consistency.

comparison.onlyPromptDescription: Without a reference, the shared prompt alone does not reliably achieve the intended game's visual style or quality.
comparison.withReferenceDescription: Generated with the same prompt and a reference, producing a result more consistent with the game's visual style and quality.

tilesets.heading: Split tilesets by construction rules.
tilesets.intro: A tileset is a working palette, not every environment asset from the same game. Keep tiles together when they share a grid, placement rules, and a purpose. Split them when those rules change.
tilesets.gridTitle: Share a grid, boundaries, and placement rules
tilesets.gridBody: Floor, wall, and edge tiles belong in the same tileset when they snap to the same grid, describe the same scale, and share collision and rotation rules. For example, a 16 x 16 grass tile can form one terrain tileset with its center, straight edge, outer corner, inner corner, cliff, and water-edge variants. Keep every variant needed for a continuous boundary together; otherwise, the pieces needed to complete a shape become hard to find.
tilesets.purposeTitle: Split by purpose and material boundaries
tilesets.purposeBody: Terrain, architecture, and interior assets can share a visual style while serving different construction tasks, so they work better as separate tilesets: terrain for outdoor ground, architecture for walls, roofs, and exterior structure, and interiors for floors, furniture, and fixtures. Keep repeatable ground, walls, and borders in a base tileset; move flowers, cracks, signs, and other optional details into a decoration tileset so the base layout stays separate from visual variation. Grass, snow, desert, and cave tiles can also be split by material when each tileset has a complete set of centers, edges, and corners. When two materials must meet directly, keep their transition tiles with the matching boundary pieces.
tilesets.multiBody: Keep a bed, tree, shopfront, or large rock as one named item that occupies several grid cells. Do not split it into unrelated pieces unless each piece must be placed independently. A complete item preserves its silhouette and avoids accidental gaps when it is moved or edited.
tilesets.check1: Do these tiles work together to build the same part of a scene?
tilesets.check2: Do they use the same grid size, scale, collision, and rotation rules?
tilesets.check3: Are all neighboring edges, corners, and material transitions available in the same tileset?
tilesets.check4: Can optional decoration be removed without breaking the map's readable structure?
tilesets.conclusion: If the answer is yes to most of these questions, keep the tiles together. If they require different construction steps or placement rules, create separate tilesets.
